title: He Bowled Six Dot Balls When Sri Lanka Needed a Run a Ball. On Debut, Anukul Roy Won India A the Match.
excerpt: India A beat Sri Lanka A by 8 runs in a high-scoring thriller in Dambulla. Anukul Roy's 10-1-49-2 was the decisive spell — a maiden over in the 38th over that turned a cruise into a collapse.
body:
In the 38th over of Sri Lanka A's chase, the equation was simple. They needed roughly a run a ball. Their middle order was set. The Indian bowlers had been leaking boundaries for the best part of fifteen overs. The game was drifting away from Tilak Varma's side as surely as the evening light was fading over the Rangiri Dambulla International Stadium.

Tilak threw the ball to Anukul Roy. It was Roy's India A debut. He was 27 years old, a left-arm spinner from Jharkhand who had waited years for an opportunity at this level. What happened next changed the match.

Six balls. Six dots. Not a single run conceded. It was the only maiden over bowled by any Indian player in the entire second innings.

The pressure that maiden created was not abstract. It was immediate, measurable, and devastating. Sri Lanka A's required rate, which had been comfortably under six an over, began to climb. Set batsmen who had been timing the ball beautifully suddenly had to take risks they had not needed to take ten minutes earlier.

In his next spell, Anukul struck twice. First, he deceived Sadeera Samarawickrama — a player with full international experience — with a slower ball that forced him to mistime a lofted shot straight to long-on. Then, as Ravindu Fernando tried to rebuild, Roy dove to his right on his follow-through and completed a brilliant caught-and-bowled dismissal.

His final figures read 10-1-49-2 at an economy of 4.90. In a match where most bowlers conceded well over six an over, those numbers were the difference between winning and losing.

India A had posted 277 for 6 in their fifty overs, built around Ruturaj Gaikwad's composed century — 101 runs from an innings that mixed classical strokeplay with calculated aggression — and captain Tilak Varma's fluent 60. But for much of Sri Lanka A's reply, those runs looked insufficient.

Sri Lanka A captain Sahan Arachchige was batting with authority, finding boundaries at will and keeping his side ahead of the required rate. Their experienced players — Arachchige, Samarawickrama, Avishka Fernando — had all spent time at the crease. The chase was proceeding exactly as the hosts would have scripted it.

What Roy did was interrupt that script. A maiden over against a set batsman on a good batting surface, at a crucial juncture, is an act of nerve as much as skill. To do it on debut, with the match slipping away, requires something beyond technique. It requires the kind of composure that cannot be coached.

India A eventually won by 8 runs. The margin is deceptively close — in a match where 277 was chased to within striking distance, 8 runs is the width of one mishit or one dropped catch. Roy's intervention ensured that those fine margins fell India's way.

For diaspora cricket fans tracking the next generation of Indian cricketers, the Dambulla tri-series — also featuring Afghanistan A — is an important staging ground. Several of the players in this squad are in active contention for senior India berths. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the 15-year-old who won the IPL Orange Cap with 776 runs at a strike rate of 237, opened the batting. Tilak Varma, the captain, is already a fixture in multiple India squads.

But the player who made the difference on Monday was not one of the headline names. It was a 27-year-old from Jharkhand, playing his first match in India A colours, who bowled six dot balls when his team needed them most.

Anukul Roy received his India A cap earlier that morning. By the evening, he had earned his next one.
